On this page (10)


Getting paid starts one step earlier than most people think. It starts at the hour: a row that knows which client it belongs to and what that client's rate is. Once every hour carries those two facts, the invoice is arithmetic your workspace can do on its own, and "get paid for everything you actually did" stops being a monthly reconstruction exercise.


## An Hour Becomes an Invoice in Four Moves


The full path from logged time to money in the bank is four moves: capture the hour, attach the client and rate, approve the period, raise the invoice. Every tool in this category does move one. What decides whether you get paid for your whole month is whether moves two through four happen automatically or get rebuilt by hand every thirty days.


Notice the last edge. When the row flips to Paid, the workspace keeps the rate, the turnaround, and the client's payment history, so the next quote you write starts from evidence instead of memory. That loop is[Workspace DNA](https://www.taskade.com/learn/genesis/workspace-dna) doing its job: Memory feeds Intelligence, Intelligence triggers Execution, Execution writes new Memory.

## Your Rate and Your Billable Share Set the Ceiling


Your income ceiling is your effective rate multiplied by the hours you can genuinely sell, and the second number is almost always lower than the number of hours you work. A 160-hour month at a 60 percent billable share leaves 96 sellable hours. Price against 160 and you will miss the target by a third no matter how hard the month felt.


```text
BILLABLE MATH  (one person, one month)    Target monthly revenue          $12,000     Working hours in the month          160     Realistic billable share            60%   ->   96 hours                                      ─────────────────────     Required effective rate      $12,000 / 96   =   $125/hr
Log 96 hours at $125 .............. $12,000    on target     Log 96, invoice only 78 ........... $ 9,750    the gap is untracked work     Raise the share to 70% (112 hrs) .. $14,000    same rate, more sold
```


The bottom two lines are the whole argument for tracking in the same place you bill. The 18-hour gap is not laziness; it is work that happened in a call, a review, or a scope change that never became a row. When logging an hour takes one tap inside the workspace where the client already lives, the gap closes on its own. The[Meeting Cost Calculator](https://www.taskade.com/blog/meeting-cost-calculator) attacks the same math from the other end by pricing the hours meetings quietly consume.

## The Automation Raises the Invoice When the Period Closes


A[schedule trigger](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/schedule) fires on the last day of the billing period, reads the approved time entries for each client, and hands them to an invoice step that drafts and sends the PDF through Gmail or Outlook. Automations run as a bounded loop over the items you point them at, so a monthly run touches this month's rows and then stops.


Three steps do most of the work:


1. **Schedule** — fire on the 1st, or on a project completion[trigger](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/triggers) if you bill per milestone.
2. **Draft and send** — the invoice action builds the PDF and emails it.[Automate Invoices, Licenses, and Receipts](https://www.taskade.com/learn/genesis/invoice-automation) is the step-by-step build.
3. **Collect** — a[Stripe Checkout Session](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/stripe-checkout) step returns a hosted payment URL you drop into the email or a pay button in the app, with no backend to stand up. When payment lands, the row flips to Paid.


The reminder branch matters more than the send. Unpaid invoices are usually forgotten, not refused, and a nudge at 7, 14, and 30 days recovers most of them without an awkward phone call.[Vibe Payments with Stripe](https://www.taskade.com/blog/vibe-payments-stripe) and[AI Invoice Automation](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-invoice-automation) go deeper on the payment half;[Estimate to Invoice](https://www.taskade.com/blog/estimate-to-invoice) covers the quote before the first hour, and[Automate Accounting and Bookkeeping](https://www.taskade.com/blog/automate-accounting-bookkeeping) covers where the numbers go afterward. Browse[ready-made automations](https://www.taskade.com/automate) and[Stripe flows](https://www.taskade.com/automate/stripe) , or connect the finance tools you already run through[100+ bidirectional integrations](https://www.taskade.com/integrations) .

## Frequently Asked Questions


How do I turn tracked hours into an invoice?


Log each hour as a row carrying a date, a client, a duration, and a rate. Table view multiplies duration by rate and sums the billable total per client as you go. When the billing period closes, a scheduled automation reads the approved rows, drafts the invoice, and emails the PDF. Nothing gets copied between tools, because the hour and the invoice live on the same record.


What is the fastest way to start tracking billable time?


Clone a working app instead of starting from an empty page. The[Time Tracker Tool](https://www.taskade.com/share/apps/kz33nmpsddj323lb) and the[Invoice Generator](https://www.taskade.com/share/apps/v71ywf2zs5bu9a5m) are both live, and cloning gives you the full build rather than a screenshot. Rename the clients, swap in your rates, and you have a usable tracker in under fifteen minutes.


Can one workspace replace a timer app, a spreadsheet, and a billing tool?


Yes, and that is the point. Taskade Genesis holds the time entries, the client rates, the rollup, and the invoice automation together, so nothing is re-keyed at a handoff. One workspace keeps the rate, the pace, and the payment history in the same place, which is what makes your next quote more accurate than your last one.


How do I calculate a billable rate that covers my costs?


Divide your target revenue by the hours you can realistically bill, not the hours you work. A 160-hour month at a 60 percent billable share leaves 96 sellable hours, so a $12,000 target needs an effective rate of $125 an hour. Track the billable share alongside the entries and the number stops being a guess.


Which project view is best for reviewing timesheets?


Table view, because it shows every entry as a row with date, client, hours, rate, and status, and sums the column for you. Taskade ships seven views in total: List, Board, Calendar, Table, Mind Map, Gantt, and Org Chart. Calendar view is the fastest way to see where a week actually went, and Board view is useful for moving entries from Draft to Approved to Invoiced.


Can an automation raise the invoice on its own?


Yes. A schedule trigger fires on the last day of the billing period, the automation reads the approved entries per client, and an invoice action drafts and sends the PDF through Gmail or Outlook. Automations run as a bounded loop over the items you point them at, so a monthly run covers this month's rows and stops. Reminder steps can nudge an unpaid invoice at 7, 14, and 30 days.


Can clients see their own hours without emailing me?


Yes. Publish the tracker as a client-facing app, turn on app sign-in, then switch on private per-user data so each client sees only their own entries, totals, and invoice status. Those sign-ins are managed separately from your workspace seats, so a client never uses a seat and never enters your workspace.


How do I collect payment once the invoice is out?


Add a[Stripe Checkout Session](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/stripe-checkout) step to the automation. It returns a hosted Stripe payment URL you can put straight into the invoice email or behind a pay button in the app, with no backend to build. When the payment lands, the row flips to Paid and the dashboard total updates on its own.

Do I need to know how to code to build this?


No. You describe the tracker in plain language and Taskade Genesis generates the fields, the views, the interface, and the automations. Taskade EVE drafts the invoice copy in your wording. Everything after that is editing rows and dragging steps, which is why a solo consultant and a ten-person studio can both run this without an engineer.

Yes. The published app runs in a mobile browser and in the Taskade apps, so an hour gets logged where the work ends rather than at a desk hours later. That single habit is usually worth more than any rate increase, because it closes the gap between hours worked and hours invoiced.

Every cycle leaves the workspace knowing more about your rates, your pace, and how fast each client actually pays, so the next quote is sharper than the last.
